One thing I sort of wished was touched on a little more: the concept of country is surprisingly modern. Modern international relations theory tends to trace the concept back to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, but honestly, even that is really too early.

The other problem you run into is that, in most non-state societies (in the Weberian sense of "monopoly on the legitimate use of force"), political linkages tend to be fragile and based more on personal ties so that a Big Man's successor may well repudiate the alliances and homages the Big Man makes. Which makes it hard to draw maps, because is Burgundy a part of France? The Duke of Burgundy is as often as not fighting the French king.

But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.
Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.
It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).

comments.author: chr15m

Every dot in these graphs is composed of multiple benchmarks smooshed together.
Benchmarks are by definition a curated set of things that can be measured and evaluated.
Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on.
The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on feedback loops made of those exact measurements, and synthesized data representing further measurements (literally benchmaxing).
What is not shown in these graphs are the set of things that intelligence can do, which are difficult, expensive or impossible to measure and evaluate.
That set of things is much larger than the set of benchmarks represented in the graph.
Therefore the post is misleading in the sense that the "superintelligence" being targeted is "jagged" to use Karpathy's term, and we infact already have jagged superintelligence (calculators, compilers, Bayesian spam classifiers, etc.)
We are witnessing a profound explosion of much more jagged superintelligence, restricted to the exact domains that can be (expensively) RL'ed on.

comments.author: NaiveEmpiricist
comments.text:
Norvig (and Chomsky) are talking at cross purposes.
Norvig confuses engineering for science. If an engineer wants something that works (and guarantees that it will work) then you use the most effective tool available to achieve that goal. No problem there. But there's absolutely no reason to think that tells you anything scientific about the phenomenon you're modeling. For example, aeronautical engineering says very little about how birds fly. And - currently relevant - LLMs learn to use and understand language, but they use millions of times more training data, and millions of times more computing power, than a child does. So an LLM may be a great technology, but it's probably not a good model for how humans learn and use language.
Chomsky OTOH doesn't see any use for statistics in science, at least not in linguistics. Fortunately for the field of linguistics, Chomsky's influence in linguistics is waning and linguists are beginning to use statistical tools to do science.

I believe this conclusion is flawed. The author argues:
1) Unitree robots are largely made by hand.

comments.author: YuechenLi
comments.text:
I don't really follow the logic in the article at all:
The argument is that Unitree's assembly process is currently very manual because there is no incentive to automate, which is because labor cost isn't the bottleneck here, where in the US labor cost are much higher, therefore the US will have incentive to automate more. Those are reasonable so far, until you try to use that as a conclusion that this is why the West will win?
First of all, what does he think the other 92% of the cost of manufacturing is? A small portion of that is materials and electricity, but the biggest part of the remaining cost is assembly tooling/fixtures for the assembly line, and a fully automated assembly line is much, much more expensive compared to a semi-automated or manual production line.
In other words: it's not that Unitree couldn't build fully automated assembly lines if they wanted to, but spending tens of millions of dollars fully automated assembly line that takes up floor space and requires even more labor for manual maintenance for a product that is only being produced by the hundreds to thousands in quantity every month rather than millions simply does not make economic sense to begin with.

In addition it keeps track of counters for various things (cache misses, interrupts, etc). Correlation refers to making sure the counter values reported by the sim are within some ballpark of the same values on a real chip.
